     ENGINEERS, et al.,                                                       
11                                                                             

                    Defendant(s).                                             
12                                                                             

13        In the Court’s order granting in part Plaintiffs’ motion for summary judgment, finding 
14   Nationwide Permit (“NWP”) 56 to be unlawful, the Court found that more information was needed 
15   to determine the appropriate remedy.  Dkt. No. 71 at 23–25.  The Court ordered the parties to meet 
16   and confer and propose a briefing schedule on remedy.  Id.  The parties complied with this 
17   instruction, and the briefing on remedy is complete.  See Dkt. Nos. 75, 77, 79, 81, 83, 84. 
18        Where a court finds an agency action to be unlawful, the presumptive remedy is a vacatur 
19   of the agency action.  All. for the Wild Rockies v. U.S. Forest Serv., 907 F.3d 1105, 1121 (9th Cir. 
20   2018).  “Where a court holds an agency action unlawful, vacatur and remand is the default remedy 
21   under the [Administrative Procedure Act], but the court retains equitable discretion in ‘limited 
22   circumstances’ to remand a decision without vacatur while the agency corrects its errors.”  Mont. 
23   Wildlife Fed. v. Haaland, 127 F.4th 1, 50 (9th Cir. 2025) (quoting Pollinator Stewardship Council 
24   v. EPA, 806 F.3d 520, 532 (9th Cir. 2015)).   In considering whether vacatur is appropriate, a court 
1   must balance the seriousness of the agency’s errors against the “disruptive consequences” of a 
2   vacatur.  Cal. Cmtys. Against Toxics v. EPA, 688 F.3d 989, 992 (9th Cir. 2012). 
3        During the parties’ meet and confer, Defendants disclosed that six projects have been 

4   approved under NWP 56 and that no pre-construction notices are pending.  Dkt. No. 79 at 9–10.  
5   With that context in mind, Plaintiffs request a prospective vacatur only, meaning that the six 
6   existing verifications may remain in place and any future projects must undergo individual 
7   permitting rather than approval via NWP 56.  Dkt. No. 81 at 8, 16. Dkt. No. 84 at 6 n.7.   
8        Defendants, on the other hand, contend that remand without vacatur is the appropriate 
9   remedy.  Dkt. No. 79 at 11.  Specifically, Defendants suggest that a prospective vacatur requiring 
10   individual permitting would be “needlessly disruptive” to potential “proponents of prospective 
11   projects to be located far away from where Plaintiffs’ members reside, work, travel, or recreate, as 
12   such project proponents may need to apply for individual permits—even for activities that could 

13   not conceivably cause Plaintiffs harm.”  Dkt. No. 83 at 6.                
14        The Court finds that any potential disruption of this sort is not “needless”; in fact, requiring 
15   future permits to be approved individually (rather than via NWP 56) would alleviate some of the 
16   Court’s concerns as described in the summary judgment order.  See Dkt. No. 71 at 17–18.  And, 
17   as Plaintiffs note, because NWP 56 is scheduled to expire in 2026 in any event, “any economic 
18   reliance interests on the current nationwide permit would be short-lived regardless of vacatur.”  
19   Dkt. No. 84 at 6 n.8.  Because no economic or environmental disruption to current facilities would 
20   result from a prospective vacatur, and because any disruption to future facilities is speculative and 
21   minimized by the upcoming expiration of NWP 56, the Court finds that this is not one of the 
22   “limited circumstances” where remand without vacatur is warranted.  Although Defendants 

23   question (Dkt. Nos. 79, 83) whether the errors identified by the Court are sufficiently serious as to 
24                                                                             
1   warrant vacatur, and/or whether the Court correctly found that Plaintiffs had standing to bring this 
2   action, the Court’s prior order finding NWP 56 unlawful is nonetheless the law of the case.   
3        As to the narrow issue remaining to be resolved—the appropriate remedy for the unlawful 

4   agency action—the Court finds that the prospective vacatur as of the date of this order, as requested 
5   by Plaintiffs, is the appropriate remedy.  The Court will enter judgment in accordance with this 
6   order and thereafter this case will be administratively closed.           
7        Dated this 17th day of March, 2025.

14        This matter comes before the Court on Defendants’ motion to limit judicial review to the 
15   administrative record.  Dkt. No. 39.  For the following reasons, the Court denies the motion. 
16        Plaintiffs contend that Defendant U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ issuance of Nationwide 
17   Permit 56, which authorizes commercial finfish mariculture facilities to place structures or perform 
18   work in navigable waters of the United States, violates several statutes as well as the property 
19   clause of the United States Constitution.  See Dkt. No. 29 at 2.  The parties agree that the Court’s 
20   review of the agency decision is subject to an “arbitrary and capricious” standard of review.  See 
21   Dkt. No. 30 at 4, Dkt. No. 41 at 2.  The parties also agree that most of the statutory claims and 
22   constitutional claims should be decided based on the Court’s review of the administrative record 
23                                                                             
24                                                                             
1   that was before the agency decisionmaker at the time of the challenged agency action.  See Dkt. 
2   No. 29 at 2 (citing 5 U.S.C. § 706).                                      
3        The parties disagree, however, as to the scope of judicial review on Plaintiffs’ Endangered 

4   Species Act (“ESA”) claim, which is brought under the ESA’s citizen-suit provision (16 U.S.C.  
5   § 1540(g)(1)).  Plaintiffs contend (Dkt. No. 41) that the Court’s review of their ESA citizen-suit 
6   claim need not be strictly limited to the administrative record, while Defendants argue (Dkt. No. 
7   39) that the documents Plaintiffs intend to introduce do not fall into the well-established, narrow 
8   exceptions to the general rule against considering extra-record evidence in actions reviewing an 
9   agency decision pursuant to the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”).  On this issue, Plaintiffs 
10   have the better argument.                                                 
11        The Ninth Circuit has distinguished between the standard of review borrowed from the 
12   APA and applied to ESA claims, and the scope of review in ESA citizen-suit cases.  See W. 

13   Watersheds Project v. Kraayenbrink, 632 F.3d 472, 497 (9th Cir. 2011), abrogated on other 
14   grounds as recognized in Cottonwood Env’t L. Ctr. v. U.S. Forest Serv., 789 F.3d 1075, 1089 (9th 
15   Cir. 2015). With respect to the latter, the Court explained that extra-record evidence may be 
16   considered in certain limited circumstances:                              
17        As we explained in [Washington Toxics Coalition v. Environmental Protection 
         Agency, 413 F.3d 1024, 1034 (9th Cir. 2005)] the APA applies only where there is 
18        “no other adequate remedy in a court,” 5 U.S.C. § 704, and – because the ESA 
         provides a citizen suit remedy – the APA does not apply in such actions.  Therefore, 
19        under  Washington  Toxics  Coalition  we  may  consider  evidence  outside  the 
         administrative record for the limited purposes of reviewing Plaintiffs’ ESA claim. 
20                                                                             
     Id.  Contrary to Defendants’ claims, Karuk Tribe of California v. U.S. Forest Service, 681 F.3d 
21                                                                             
    1006, 1017 (9th Cir. 2012) (en banc), did not change this outcome.  In Karuk Tribe, the en banc 
22                                                                             
    Court recited the familiar APA standard of review applicable to ESA cases but did not otherwise 
23                                                                             
    discuss whether the scope of judicial review of an ESA citizen-suit claim is limited to the 
24                                                                             
1   administrative record.  Id. (“Because this is a record review case, we may direct that summary 
2   judgment be granted to either party based upon our review of the administrative record.”).  Nor 
3   did Karuk Tribe discuss either Kraayenbrink or Washington Toxics Coalition with respect to this 

4   issue, let alone expressly overrule them on this point.                   
5        Furthermore, the Ninth Circuit has again recently reaffirmed that extra-record evidence 
6   may be considered in an ESA citizen suit.  See Nat’l Fam. Farm Coal. v. U.S. Env’t Prot. Agency, 
7   966 F.3d 893, 926 & n.11 (9th Cir. 2020) (“Although the Interim Report is not in the administrative 
8   record, we can consider it ‘for the limited purpose[] of reviewing [Petitioners’] ESA claim.’” 
9   (quoting Kraayenbrink, 632 F.3d at 497)).  Defendants attempt to distinguish National Family 
10   Farm Coalition on the grounds that the scope of review was addressed sua sponte, without the 
11   benefit of the parties’ briefing.  Dkt. No. 39 at 12 n.2.  Contrary to Defendants’ claim, however, 
12   National Family Farm Coalition does not purport to “overrule” other Ninth Circuit authority; it 

13   instead explicitly relies upon and quotes Kraayenbrink to explain its consideration of extra-record 
14   evidence in reviewing an ESA claim.  See 966 F.3d at 926 n.11.            
15        Thus, the Court rejects Defendants’ argument that binding Ninth Circuit authority strictly 
16   limits the Court’s review to the administrative record in this case.  Although the Court’s review 
17   may not necessarily be confined to the administrative record, the Court must nonetheless scrutinize 
18   any attempt to introduce extra-record evidence. The Court will consider only relevant, admissible 
19   evidence, with only limited latitude to consider evidence post-dating the challenged agency 
20   decision in resolving the dispositive motion(s) filed in this case.  See, e.g., Friends of the 
21   Clearwater v. Higgins, 523 F. Supp. 3d 1213, 1219-23 (D. Ida. 2021).  The Court will not take 
22   judicial notice of government documents for the truth of the matter asserted when the facts are in 

23   dispute.  Id.  Because the Court cannot determine without briefing from the parties whether the 
24                                                                             
1                                                                             
    extra-record documents that Plaintiffs seek to introduce comport with these guidelines,1 the Court 
2   will address any concerns related to the extra-record evidence in the context of resolving the 
3   anticipated dispositive motion(s) and/or a motion to supplement the record.  
4        For these reasons, the Court DENIES Defendants’ motion.  Dkt. No. 39. 
5        Dated this 20th day of October, 2023.

13                                                                             
         The parties’ cross-motions for summary judgment in this action require the Court to review 
14                                                                             
    Nationwide Permit (“NWP”) 56, issued by Defendant United States Army Corps of Engineers 
15                                                                             
    (“the Corps”) to authorize the installation of structures to be used in finfish aquaculture operations 
16                                                                             
    in United States waters.  The Court’s review of NWP 56 indicates that the Corps issued the permit 
17                                                                             
    without fully complying with the procedural safeguards imposed by the Rivers and Harbors Act 
18                                                                             
    of 1899 (“RHA”) and the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”).  The Court therefore 
19                                                                             
    finds that the Corps violated the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”), and Plaintiffs’ motion is 
20                                                                             
    granted in that respect.  The Court finds, however, that Defendants are entitled to summary 
21                                                                             
    judgment on Plaintiffs’ claims asserting that Defendants acted outside of their authority in issuing 
22                                                                             
    NWP 56.  Although the Court concludes NWP 56 is unlawful, more information is needed before 
23                                                                             
    the Court can determine the appropriate remedy, as explained herein.      
24                                                                             
1                           I.  BACKGROUND                                    
2        In May 2020, President Trump issued an executive order titled “Promoting American 
3   Seafood Competitiveness and Economic Growth.”  Exec. Order No. 13,921, 85 Fed. Reg. 28,471 

4   (May 7, 2020).  This order required that, among other things, within 90 days the Secretary of the 
5   Army develop and propose for public comment an NWP authorizing finfish aquaculture activities 
6   in United States waters.  Id. at 28,473–74.                               
7        The Corps narrowed the scope of the proposed NWP to authorize only the structures to be 
8                                                                             
    used in finfish aquaculture activities rather than the activities themselves (NWP0024401), and with 
9   that limitation applied, the Corps found that the permit would cause no more than “minimal” 
10   environmental impacts and was therefore suitable to be issued as a general permit.  NWP002436–
11   NWP002519.  The Corps’ decision document contains an environmental assessment (“EA”) 
12   concluding  that  the  NWP  would  cause  no  significant  impact  to  the  quality  of  the  human 
13   environment, and that as a result of that finding, a full environmental impact statement (“EIS”) 
14   was not needed.  NWP002518.  The Corps’ review also determined that the activities permitted 
15   under this NWP would not impact any species listed in the Endangered Species Act (“ESA”), and 
16   thus the Corps found it was not required by the ESA to consult with other federal agencies before 
17   issuing the permit.  See NWP002514–NW002518.                              
18        NWP 56 was issued in January 2021, and Plaintiffs (a collection of nonprofit and other 
19   organizations) filed this action against the Corps and its lieutenant general (referred to collectively 
20   herein as “the Corps”) in November 2022 to challenge NWP 56 and request its vacatur.  Dkt. No. 
21   1.  Plaintiffs amended their complaint in January 2023.  Dkt. No. 14.  After the administrative

9   A.   Legal Standards on Summary Judgment                                  
10        Summary judgment is appropriate only when “the movant shows that there is no genuine 
11   dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.”  Fed. R. 
12   Civ. P. 56(a).  The Court does not make credibility determinations or weigh the evidence at this 
13   stage.  Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 255 (1986).  The sole inquiry is “whether 
14   the evidence presents a sufficient disagreement to require submission to a jury or whether it is so 
15   one-sided that one party must prevail as a matter of law.”  Id. at 251–52.   
16   B.   Plaintiffs Have Standing to Challenge NWP 56.                        
17        In order to establish standing to sue under Article III of the Constitution, a plaintiff must 
18   establish that it has “(1) suffered an injury in fact, (2) that is fairly traceable to the challenged 
19   conduct of the defendant, and (3) that is likely to be redressed by a favorable judicial decision.”  
20   Spokeo,  Inc.  v.  Robins,  578  U.S.  330,  338  (2016).    The  injury  must  be  “‘concrete  and 
21   particularized’ and ‘actual or imminent, not conjectural or hypothetical.’”  Id. at 339 (quoting 
22   Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555, 560 (1992)).

21   C.   The Corps Inadequately Assessed NWP 56’s Impacts.                    

22        1.  The Corps Is Obligated to Consider the Impacts of Its Actions.   

23        The Corps issues permits under several statutory authorities, including Section 10 of the 
24   RHA (33 U.S.C. § 403).  The Corps is a “highly decentralized organization” that delegates most 
1   of the authority for administering its regulatory programs to engineers at the regional division and 
2   local district level.  See 33 C.F.R. §§ 320.1(a)(2), 325.8(b)–(c).  “Reducing unnecessary paperwork 
3   and delays is a continuing Corps goal.”  Id. § 320.1(a)(4).               

4        Because the Corps receives a number of Section 10 permit applications each year, it relies 
5   on general permits such as NWPs to manage its regulatory docket and focus its limited resources 
6   on projects that may cause more than minimal impacts.  See 33 C.F.R. § 322.2(f).  NWPs are 
7   “designed to regulate with little, if any, delay or paperwork certain activities having minimal 
8   impacts.”  Id. § 330.1(b).  NWPs set forth the specific terms and conditions that must be followed 
9   in order to obtain authorization for activities under that permit.  See, e.g., id. §§ 330.1(c), 330.2(h). 
10        In order to determine which projects are suitable for authorization on a general level via 
11   nationwide permit, the Corps’ chief of engineers must conduct a predictive environmental analysis 
12   at the national level to determine whether the category of activities authorized by a proposed permit 

13   will  be  “substantially  similar  in  nature  and  cause  only  minimal  individual  or  cumulative 
14   environmental impacts” over the permit’s five-year duration.  33 C.F.R. §§ 322.2(f)(1), 330.5(b).  
15   A determination that a proposed project will have “minimal impacts” must comply with the Corps’ 
16   regulations, which require the Corps to consider certain public interest factors.  See id. § 320.4(a).  
17   Specifically, Corps regulations provide that “[t]he decision whether to issue a permit will be based 
18   on an evaluation of the probable impacts, including cumulative impacts, of the proposed activity 
19   and its intended use on the public interest.”  Id. § 320.4(a)(1).  The public interest review process 
20   also addresses mitigation measures needed to avoid, minimize, rectify, reduce, or compensate for 
21   resource losses resulting from authorized projects.  Id. § 320.4(r).      
22        In addition to the Corps’ obligation to analyze the impacts of a Section 10 nationwide 

23   permit before issuance, NEPA also requires federal agencies, including the Corps, “to analyze the 
24   environmental impact of their proposals and actions.”  Coal. to Protect Puget Sound Habitat v. 
1   U.S. Army Corps of Eng’rs, 417 F. Supp. 3d 1354, 1357 (W.D. Wash. 2019) (quoting O’Reilly v. 
2   U.S. Army Corps of Eng’rs, 477 F.3d 225, 228 (5th Cir. 2007)).  Federal agencies must first 
3   complete an EA of their proposed actions.  See 40 C.F.R. § 1501.5.  If they cannot state in an EA 

4   that their proposed action will not have significant effects then they must go on to prepare a more 
5   detailed, comprehensive EIS.  See 40 C.F.R. § 1501.6.                     
6        A court may set aside an agency action under the APA if the action is “arbitrary, capricious, 
7   an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law[.]”  5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A).  This 
8   standard is deferential, and courts should uphold an agency’s decision    
9        unless the agency has relied on factors which Congress has not intended it to 
         consider, entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the problem, offered an 
10        explanation for its decision that runs counter to the evidence before the agency, or 
         is so implausible that it could not be ascribed to a difference in view or the product 
11        of agency expertise.                                                 

12   Friends of Santa Clara River, 887 F.3d at 920–21 (quoting Nat’l Ass’n of Home Builders v. Defs. 
13   of Wildlife, 551 U.S. 644, 658 (2007)).
